8257:
Just to make your BASIC simpler and easier to understand, you could do it this way.
10 FOR X=0TO !FFF
20 @(X)=%(X+!2000)
30 NEXT X
40 PRINT "IN RAM";PRINT "PUT @(0),!7FF TO SAVE

You don't need end quotes if the text is at the end of the line. The STOP command is unnecessary if the last command is in the last line. you only need a stop command if you have more program after the place you put the STOP.
Ken
P.S. You could POKE to, say, %(!9000), but that would add 6 bytes. If you made it all one line, you would save 2 bytes for each line number. The "GO" would be a wash because you need to add a semicolon between each command.

> Brett, can you elaborate on this program a little bit?

My goal was to teach folks how to use the vertical interrupt routines to move graphics like the cartridges, but from BASIC!

All the game 'logic' could be done easily in BASIC, and the graphics could be done in machine code with the vertical interrupts so the graphics updates were smooth... The vertical interrupts were so you knew you were moving data in memory when the display scan output was not reading from the memory (that conflict is what causes the flickering graphic updates).

with '=' to display "-1" in Decimal then switching to Hex shows as
"FFFF FFFF FFFF FFFF". Change to Word for "FFFF" or ignore extras.

.
Bally BASICs only know -32768 through 32767 so anyting outside that
range is wrong. Hex numbers from 8000 through FFFF are how negative
Decimal numbers are stored. Converting those to Decimal require you
to subtract the magic number "65536" to get correct Base 10 number.

Well, since MP3 uses lossy compression, you basically choose the trade-off between quality and size.  I uploaded 192kbps, which is pretty standard.  But some of the recordings are quite long, which leads to the large size.  There are also other audio formats.  Ogg Vorbis is said to have good quality at lower file sizes, but it's not nearly as popular as MP3.

Here's something even more interesting I found.  I tried FLAC, which is a lossless audio compression format, and was actually able to get smaller file sizes than the 192kbps MP3's!  I think FLAC works particularly well for spoken audio, since there's a lot of silence.  The files still aren't small, though.

http://flac.sourceforge.net/

So, for example, the Astrocade meeting:

WAV:  114MB
MP3 (192kbps):  62MB
FLAC:  49MB

I can re-encode them if you want.  It just comes down to size vs. quality vs. accessibility.

Paul

I would suspect that the high price probably scared them off, just like the
high price of the Keyboard Component scared off Mattel in 1981/2, causing
them to go to plan B for the Intellivision with the ECS. Once you hit $1000,
even in the late 70's, you were competing with full featured pure computers,
and an add-on for what was ostensibly a game console (or at least a device
already with an identity crisis) would have been a tough sell at that price.
Even the Imagination Machine add-on for the APF MP1000 was targeting a
sub-$500 price in June 1979, and that's surely the most direct comparison
that could be made to what an add-on for the Astrocade would have involved.
It appears that in May 1980 the Imagination Machine was selling for around
$600, so they didn't quite make that price point, but for comparison
purposes, an Atari 800 (not 400) with 48K RAM was selling for around $1,000
(a TI-99/4, not 4a, with monitor, sold for around $1150 with 16K RAM).

F0

PLAYIT


PLAYIT

NEXT I

SETUP

ARRAY.INT SONG,20
FOR I1 TO 19
SONG(I)-7
NEXT I
ARRAY.STR SCALE,22

NEXT I

===========================

I notice heavy use of left arrow () I'm guessing in place of = or more modernly == (assignment).
Equals (=) is used for comparison as in languages where == is assignment.
As the left allow is no longer part of the ASCII code, it would be hard to reimplement this language exactly as was...

I also notice use of /, \, and * for math notation. I can see this as Devide and Multiply arn't/wern't on terminal/computer keyboards of the time. Not sure what the other slash '\' is though...

& used for string concatination. eg: '*'&(I-14)

SCALE() is set to the musical scale....Checking my Bally AstroBASIC manual...

Divide 1-7 = Lower octive
1-7 Middle octive
Miltiply 1-7 Upper octive

I have added ten pictures of a Bally / Astrocade Hand Control.  Paul's recent pictures that I've been adding inspired me to take a few pictures of another hardware item that is surprisingly not already on the Bally Alley website.

The controllers that come with the Bally Arcade and the Astrocade are NOT  called joysticks, even though that is the name to which they are often referred.  The controllers, by both Astrocade and Bally, are called "hand controls," or, less frequently, "control handles."  The "button" on the "hand control" is called the "trigger," and the paddle-like device on the "hand control" is called the "knob."

The Bally / Astrocade console could have up to four controllers plugged in at the same time.  Each controller was numbered on the top of the knob to help help the player identify which controller was plugged into which port.  The number was only cosmetic; it did not matter which port a hand controller was plugged into.

The article that Richard Degler found, "Chip Set Marks Difference Between Arcade and Home Games," is a good, fast read.  Infoworld is still around today, but I've never read an article like this before-- nor have I seen an issue with a GAME on the cover.  Heck, the news magazine doesn't even have photographs on the cover anymore.

Here are comments on the article:

>>
Playing Galaxian or Space Invaders on an Apple never seems to have the same spirit of the arcade game. The controls seem sluggish and the action seems slower.
>>

I'm not Apple expert, but as the machine advanced in years, didn't the quality of the arcade translations get better?

>>
The difference [between computers with slow or fast graphics], then, is not in the display, but in the use of dedicated chip sets and a Z80 to supervise those chips.
>>

It's weird that he uses the Z80 here.  It certainly isn't the only computer with a dedicated graphics chipset.  The Atari 8-bit computers had that for YEARS, and they are 6502 based.  So, it's not the main processor that makes the difference, but the chipset itself.  I've always thought of the Atari Jaguar as a perfect example of this.  It's got a 6800 CPU, but the chipset does amazing things.  I've read that all the CPU for the Jaguar is supposed to take care is controller input.

>>
[DNA] developed and patented an important custom chip set that is used in many arcade games.
>>

Not THAT many.  Just six released games, plus a few other games that were not released.  Does anyone know the average number of games that a manufacturer is/was able to get out of an arcade chipset?

>>
This three-chip system was developed out of work done to create the famous Bally Arcade game Gunfighter.
>>

I've heard this before.  I've even seen some details about this.  I'd absolutely LOVE to read a book about the development of this, sort of in the vein of "Racing the Beam."  There is just so much history that needs to be told about DNA.  Why only a few people know about it is beyond me.  Well, really, it's NOT beyond me.  If their is nothing to read, then how WOULD people know?

The newest effort using this system is a new game being released this week called ROTO

"We've done marketing surveys on [Robby Roto] and it has the same attraction as "Pac Man," said game designer Bob Ogden. "In fact, Pac Man players prefer it."

Wow.  That's a bold statement.  I wonder who the test market for that was?  I wonder WHERE that happened?  Where?  Also, the game was program by Jay Fenton, but designed by Bob?  Or, is Bob just referred to as a generic game designer, and not the designer of Robby Roto?

The games produced at Nutting Associates are written in a FORTH-like language called TERSE. TERSE is described as a FORTH with extensions and special graphics commands.

We created a custom development environment.

We used the TRS-80 RAM expansion module as a dual-ported RAM. We had a cable that went to a cartridge that went into the Bally arcade. The other end was wired to memory.

We mapped it so the Bally was executing code that was in the RAM expansion.

All I had to do was compile the Z-80 assembler code on the TRS-80 and target the Expansion RAM for where the object code was put. Then hit reset on the Bally arcade and the Bally would execute the new code.

One side effect of this was I could read/write to cartridge RAM locations while the Bally was running. Meaning to 'tweak' the code (speed things up, slow things down), I could just write new constant values to the Expansion RAM and the cartridge would start using the new code on the fly.
